I've got a different model now, but similar concept. I got the following error for  main effects and interaction terms: lavaan WARNING: correlation between variables abxc and ab is (nearly) 1.0

messages.body_plain:
> I got the following error for  main effects and interaction terms: lavaan WARNING: correlation between variables abxc and ab is (nearly) 1.0

That is not an error message, it is a warning message (indicating something might need your attention, but the model still ran).  If I understand correctly from almost no information you provided, you have observed variables ab, c, and their product abxc.  The correlation between ab and the product term is near 1, so I would imagine c has very little variance (e.g., most values == 1), so the product term differs little from ab.  I think you can safely ignore the warning and interpret the interaction as you would in regression.

> I read about this happening when it comes to interaction based moderation and people use centering for continuous variables. I've read that when it comes to categorical variables, it can be ignored but I've also read someone mentioning that all variables must be centered.

Mean-centering doesn't change correlations among predictors, but it can minimize the correlation of each variable with their product term.  I don't think centering categorical predictors makes much sense, and it is easier to interpret the effects of dummy codes, so I would leave them as is.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Does it matter if the correlation matrix of latent variables is not positive definite with DWLS factor extraction?
messages.subject_clean: Does it matter if the correlation matrix of latent variables is not positive definite with DWLS factor extraction?
messages.body_plain:
On 01/04/2016 07:10 AM, Brent Caldwell wrote:
> lavaan WARNING: number of observations (203) too small to compute Gamma

This warning tells you that your sample size (in one group) may be too
small to get a reliable estimate of the 'Gamma' matrix (which is used
for weighting). This may affect the quality of the results. Or not. Hard
to say.

> lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive
> definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.

This is more serious. Perhaps you have negative variances? Or highly
correlated factors? In any case, this is a symptom of misfit. Again,
this may be a (small) sample problem.

> of latent variables is not positive definite, given that DWLS does not
> have to rotate the matrix?

Rotate? Rotation has nothing to do with it.

> I tried using ML, but it said that the covariance matrix of
> latent variables was not positive definite in either the smallest ethnic
> group (n=203) nor all the other ethnicities combined (n=1145) which had
> been positive definite with DWLS estimation.

DWLS is often more forgiving, but ML is not. But if both estimators give
you trouble in the smallest group, you may have to conclude that your
sample size (in that group) is just too small, given the size of your model.

> I noticed that if I restricted the analysis to subjects who had complete
> data on all variables

Given that your sample size is already small, I would hesitate to
exclude even more observations.

> hypothesis is that subjects who missed recording one or more of 'age,
> gender, ethnicity, address' were probably rushing their answering of the
> questions and not being attentive and therefore when they completed the
> psychological battery, they probably didn't consider their answers
> carefully, and may have given contradictory answers.

That would be very unfortunate. I am not sure you can repair this.

> However the difftest command has disappeared from R
> in the latest semTools package.

You should use anova() (which calls lavTestLRT) instead. The difftest
function was old and primitive, and certainly did not handle robust test
statistics.

>  As far as I can tell, the
> measurementInvariance command assumes data are continuous, not ordinal.
>   Is there a way to check for measurement invariance using ordinal data?

See the measurementInvarianceCat() function in semTools.

Yves.

--
Yves Rosseel -- http://www.da.ugent.be
Department of Data Analysis, Ghent University
http://lavaan.org

messages.body_plain:
I am working on a user-friendly batch of code that allows for simple input of information that is then passed on to Lavaan. Ideally, entering a string of basic information like correlations and passing those to Lavaan (ultimately to do various power calculations).

The issue I'm having is passing values to the model statement.

For example, if I want a model to have regression coefficients of .3 and .2, I can use the statement below

a1<-'y~ 0.3*x1 + 0.2*x2
'

That works fine but want to I want to is specify two coefficients like this:

by1<-0.3
by2<-0.2

then pass these along to the model statement (this makes the code far more flexible and simpler for non-experts)

a2<-'y~ by1*x1 + by2*x2

Doing this, however, establishes two labels (by1 and by2) but does not bring in the 0.3 and 0.2 values.

How can I accomplish this without directly entering the values as in a1?

messages.subject: Multivariate Latent Growth Curve Model with Linear and Non-Linear Curve
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate Latent Growth Curve Model with Linear and Non-Linear Curve
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to conduct a parallel growth curve of ostracism experience and symptom variable over four time points. There is a large proportion of missing data, however I would only use the completers (i.e. those who participated at every time points). To illustrate, the initial number of participant was 2359 people and the completers were 139 people.

So as a first step, I successfully fit the symptom variable on a linear curve using the growth() function and MLM estimator (and adding a quadratic curve in the model did not improve fit). Then, I successfully fit the ostracism variable on a linear curve, but the fit indices were not optimal and adding a quadratic curve did not improve fit. Also, the slope was not significant.

Because the fit was not optimal, I tried a latent curve function (syntax: i =~ 1*OES + 1*T2OES + 1*T3OES + 1*T4OES; s =~ 0*OES + 1*T2OES + NA*T3OES + NA*T4OES) with MLM estimator. I got the following warning messages:
Warning messages:
1: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
2: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.

However, using WLSM estimator made the warning messages go away and this model showed statistically significant fit improvement over the linear model.

So now I have two growth curve models for my two variables: a linear curve for symptoms (estimated with MLM) and a non-linear curve for ostracism (estimated with WLSM). A more complex problem arise when I join the two together in one model as a multivariate latent growth curve to see whether the slope is correlated to one another, and this is central to my research question.

First, I used the optimal curve model of both variables. This is the syntax for linear curve symptoms and non-linear curve ostracism:
GPOSOES3.model <- '
i1 =~ 1*F.CAPE.P + 1*T2F.CAPE.P + 1*T3F.CAPE.P + 1*T4F.CAPE.P
s1 =~ 0*F.CAPE.P + 1*T2F.CAPE.P + 2*T3F.CAPE.P + 3*T4F.CAPE.P
i2 =~ 1*OES + 1*T2OES + 1*T3OES + 1*T4OES
s2 =~ 0*OES + 1*T2OES + NA*T3OES + NA*T4OES
i1 ~~ i2
s2 ~~ s1'
GPOSOES3.fit <- growth(GPOSOES3.model, data = d, estimator = "DWLS")
But, this produced the following warning message:
Warning messages:
1: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
2: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") to investigate.
3: In lav_object_post_check(lavobject) :
  lavaan WARNING: observed variable error term matrix (theta) is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"theta") to investigate.

Changing the estimator to MLM did not solve the problem (but the theta warning goes away).

This lead me back to use a linear curve for both symptoms and ostracism:
GPOSOES2.model <- '
i1 =~ 1*F.CAPE.P + 1*T2F.CAPE.P + 1*T3F.CAPE.P + 1*T4F.CAPE.P
s1 =~ 0*F.CAPE.P + 1*T2F.CAPE.P + 2*T3F.CAPE.P + 3*T4F.CAPE.P
i2 =~ 1*OES + 1*T2OES + 1*T3OES + 1*T4OES
s2 =~ 0*OES + 1*T2OES + 2*T3OES + 3*T4OES
s1 ~~ i2
s2 ~~ i1'

messages.body_plain:
On 01/07/2016 07:00 PM, Jarrett Byrnes wrote:
> I love the ability to use the := to calculate direct and indirect
> effects and their SEs.  One question, however. Is there a way to use
> inspect or some other function to extract these variables and their SE
> for use in other applications?

For the estimate alone, you can use coef() with the "all" option (see
below) (the documentation in class?lavaan still speaks of "user", which
still works, but 'all' is more natural)

But in general, I would use the parameterEstimates() function, which
just returns a data.frame, so you can easily 'select' the ':=' rows:

set.seed(1234)
X <- rnorm(100); M <- 0.5*X + rnorm(100)
Y <- 0.2*X + 0.8*M + rnorm(100)
Data <- data.frame(X,M,Y)

model <- ' M ~ a*X
            Y ~ b*M + X
            indirect := a*b
          '
fit <- sem(model, data = Data)
summary(fit)

coef(fit, "all")
#       a        b      Y~X     M~~M     Y~~Y     X~~X indirect
#   0.474    0.888    0.236    1.054    0.898    0.999    0.421

PE <- parameterEstimates(fit)
PE[PE$op == ":=", c("est", "se")]

#     est    se
# 1 0.421 0.101

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
It sounds like you had no problem running lavaan, so I'm not sure why you posted your question here instead of the more general SEM forum SEMNET (http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html).  You are not getting error messages, just warning messages that your estimates fall outside of theoretical boundaries.  With your small sample size, you should expect to get slightly different results with different estimators (estimators are only equivalent asymptotically).

Did you do what the warnings said?  (use inspect(fit,"cov.lv <http://cov.lv/>") to investigate)  If you investigated which variances were negative, I'm guessing they will be among the same variances that were almost zero in the model without warnings:

> Variances:
>                    Estimate  Std.Err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
>     F.CAPE.P          0.045    0.015    3.065    0.002    0.045    0.271
>     T2F.CAPE.P        0.012    0.004    2.727    0.006    0.012    0.096
>     T3F.CAPE.P        0.060    0.022    2.764    0.006    0.060    0.349
>     T4F.CAPE.P        0.008    0.006    1.280    0.200    0.008    0.063
>     OES               0.545    0.170    3.211    0.001    0.545    0.410
>     T2OES             0.368    0.095    3.874    0.000    0.368    0.315
>     T3OES             0.374    0.131    2.857    0.004    0.374    0.296
>     T4OES             0.278    0.146    1.905    0.057    0.278    0.210
>     i1                0.121    0.024    4.982    0.000    1.000    1.000
>     s1                0.002    0.002    1.426    0.154    1.000    1.000
>     i2                0.784    0.177    4.434    0.000    1.000    1.000
>     s2                0.036    0.028    1.301    0.193    1.000    1.000

The ML estimator assumes all parameters have normally distributed sampling distributions, even if they have natural theoretical boundaries like (co)variances.  So when you explain most of the variance in an outcome variable (i.e., population residual variance is close to zero), sometimes you will get negative estimates of residual variance just due to sampling variability, particularly in small samples (when sampling variance is higher).  See http://dx.doi.org/10.1177/0049124112442138 for a great discussion of this, along with methods for testing whether a negative error variance estimate is due to sampling variability or misspecification.  Judging from the fact that one estimator gave you a negative estimate and another did not (assuming they are among the ones I highlighted), I would suppose the former, but that is an empirical question you can test easily with bootstrapped CIs, as described in the citation above.

As far as your sample size goes, you have thrown away a lot of data to only analyze completers.  If you haven't already, you should read some literature on modern methods for handling missing data.  FIML is available in lavaan (missing = "fiml"), including with robust correction (estimator = "MLR").  The semTools package has functions to help automate the use of auxiliary variables needed to justify the MAR assumption (see ?auxiliary), or to use multiple imputation (see ?runMI).  Here is some literature to get you started:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2009.10.001
http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/jpepsy/jst048
http://www.appliedmissingdata.com/

Terry

messages.subject: Re: sempath diagram after matrixpls.
messages.subject_clean: sempath diagram after matrixpls.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is not currently possible and although it would not be difficult to implement some kind of support for semPlot that you could use like

semPlot(matrixpls.out)

I do not think that doing so is a good idea for multiple reasons:

1) A path diagram is associated with multiple equations models, but PLS analysis does not do that. Rather, it calculates a set of weighted composites which are then used in separate regression. Presenting these results as a path diagram is likely to mislead your readers.

2) Wold’s original papers (unfortunately) used diagrams that are similar to path diagrams. In these diagrams, the composites were presented as circles, and arrows from indicators to circles were used to indicate that the composite was constructed with “Mode B” and arrows in the other direction were used for “Mode A”. This is problematic again because the reader will interpret the diagram as a factor model or a “formative model”, but that was not the idea in the original diagrams. Moreover, Mode A and Mode B are just a subset of different indicator weighting systems implemented by matrixpls and it is not clear what notation should be used for all the other systems (e.g. principal components.)

3) Some introductory articles misleadingly present PLS as a simultaneous equations technique and present the equations as well. These equations contain the following subset:

eta = beta*eta + zeta
eta = gamma*x + delta

(e.g., Chin, 1998, eq. 1, 7, 9; Fornell & Cha, 1994, eq. 2.16, 2.20, 2.24; Haenlein & Kaplan, 2004; Henseler, Ringle, & Sinkovics, 2009, eq. 1, 3, 5; Tenenhaus, Esposito Vinzi, Chatelin, & Lauro, 2005, pp. 163–166)

The semPlot diagrams do not allow such overlapping equations. But this is a minor problem compared to the fact that under the typical assumption of independent errors (zeta, delta), the model itself is impossible: beta*eta + zeta = gamma*x + delta cannot be true for any population.

4) The purpose of the matrixpls package is to educate people on what PLS does. Providing automatic path diagrams goes against this purpose.

But if you disagree, you can try to convince me otherwise. I understand that some people will consider this a bit off topic. Please let me know and I will start my own email list.

Mikko

> suggested updating lavaan, but I am using lavaan_0.5-20, R version 3.1.2.

This is another problem: you seem to have 5 categories (at least for
item11), but in group 1, the 4th category only has 1 observation, and
the last category has no observations. Therefore, we can not estimate
threshold values for this item11 in group 1.

Usually, this happens if the sample is too small (in this group), or if
the item is very skewed, or both.

The only solution is to collapse categories for those items (take
together category 4 and 5), in all groups.

You can screen your variables before the analysis using the lavTables()
function:

lavTables(dat, dim = 1)

Yves.

> I thought that other SEM programs stop when they have negative variances (or covariances)

There is nothing impossible about negative covariances.  EQS is the only software I am aware of that constrains variances to be positive by default.  This paper provides insight into why that is not a good default-idea:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.13.2.150

> I have done what you suggested, and I did found those highlighted variables to have negative SE variance from the bootstrap test. I have also tried to run the same analysis with FIML and MLR, and the results are much nicer.

Good news.  I imagine you were using WLS because you had Likert-type indicators.   FYI, robust ML provides approximately equivalent results to the more appropriate robust DWLS as long as there are at least 5 categories, but not so much with fewer categories.  This article provides good guidance about which estimator to prefer in different situations:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0029315

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Simulating standardized data - bug?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
Johannes is right - the simulateData() command throws an error if standardized regression coefficients larger than 1 are encountered, but that must be an error.
Standardized regression coefficients in MULTIPLE (but not single) regression are only bounded by the specific constellation of inter-correlations of variables, but are not strictly bounded by |1|.
Here is another counter-example (done outside lavaan):

library(MASS)
Sigma <- matrix(c(1,.95,.60,
                  .95,1,.80,
                  .80,.60,1),3,3)
d1 <- data.frame(mvrnorm(n = 1000, rep(0, 3), Sigma, empirical = TRUE))
names(d1) <- c("x1","x2","y")
var(d1) #variables are indeed standardized with mean 0 and total variance 1
lm(y~x1+x2,data=d1) #regression model with large coefficient values >1

The covariance matrix used for data-generation is standardized (mean 0, var 1), and the regression coefficients are all substantially larger than 1.

This also happens if all coefficients are negative:

cov(simulateData("y ~ .5*x + .2*z \n x ~~ .5*z",
                  standardized=TRUE,sample.nobs=100000))

This model above also implies a positive-definite correlation matrix, in which the predictors are correlated -.7, and the two correlations between predictors and outcome is -.36 each.

I looked at the R code for simulateData but can't figure out quite yet where the error lies.
Felix

messages.subject: Re: Simulating standardized data - bug?
messages.subject_clean: Simulating standardized data - bug?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all

@Felix thanks for your help. It's good to see that indeed there's nothing wrong with standardized coefficients > 1.

After digging more into this issue, I now do believe that this is a bug. The simulateData function currently attempts to standardize as follows:

- set exogenous variables to variance 1 and all residual variances to 0
- compute implied covariance matrix Sigma.hat
- set residual i to 1 - Sigma.hat[i,i]

While this does work in some cases (e.g. simple factor models), in general I believe this is not correct. Below is a derivation of how to standardize for DAG models, which is a special case but even in this case the above procedure won't work in general.

Define Beta as the matrix of standardized regression coefficients (i.e. Beta[y,z] = c for y ~ c*z); this is the same as lavaan's Beta matrix.

Then define Lambda = (I-t(Beta))^{-1}, where I is the identity matrix. Then the implied covariance matrix is

Sigma = t(Lambda) * Phi * Lambda

where Phi are the residual variances that we are looking for. Specifically, we wish to find Phi such that

diag( t(Lambda) * Phi * Lambda ) = 1

(where 1 is a vector of all ones)

diag( t(Lambda) * Phi * Lambda ) can be written as t(Lambda)^2 * v, where v = diag(Phi).

In other words, we wish to solve the equation system

t(Lambda)^2 v = 1

Plugging back in the definition of Lambda, the solution is given by

v = (t(I - Beta))^{-2}

So we need to solve a nontrivial linear equation system to find the residual variances. Also, note that this does not require any distinction between exogenous and non-exogenous covariates.

Below is code that implements this procedure, and demonstrates it on one example. Unfortunately I don't know enough about the various classes of models supported by lavaan to fix the simulateData code itself.

Best regards
Johannes

# example model where simulateData( lav, standardized=TRUE ) fails
lav <- lavaanify( "
y ~ (-.5) * x + (.25) * z
x ~ .5*U
z ~ .5*U
")

# use the equation solving approach explained above
ov.names <- vnames(lav, "ov")
Beta <- t(lavaan(lav)@Model@GLIST$beta)

vars <- solve( t(diag(nrow(Beta))-Beta)^2 ) %*% rep(1,nrow(Li))
# or use MASS::ginv instead of solve for near-singularity robustness

var.group <- which(lav$op == "~~" & lav$lhs %in% ov.names &
        lav$rhs == lav$lhs)

lav$ustart[var.group] <- vars

# check implied covariance matrix

cov(simulateData(lav,sample.nobs=1000000))

messages.subject: "lavaan WARNING: some models are based on a different set of observed variables"
messages.subject_clean: "lavaan WARNING: some models are based on a different set of observed variables"
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm doing a confirmatory factor analysis on a dataset with 405 observations of 40 variables.

I'd like to be able to compare models that make use of more or fewer of these variables, e.g.:

model1 <- 'F1 =~ A + B + C + D + E + F + G + H + I + J + K'
model2 <- 'F1 =~ A + B + C + D + E + F
F2 =~ G + H + I + J + K'
model3 <- 'F1 =~ A + B + C + D
F2 =~ E + F + G
F3 =~ H + I + J + K'
model4 <- 'F1 =~ A + B + D
F2 =~ E + G
F3 =~ I + J + K'

In reality, model1 has one factor that uses all 40 items; model2 has 2 factors that use all 40 items between them; model3 has 3 factors that use all 40 items between them; and model4 has 3 factors that use only 16 items between them.

When I compare only model1, model2, and model3 (using anova(model1, model2, model3, model4)), I find that model1 fits significantly worse than model3, which is not significantly worse than model2.  So, so far, looks like model3 is the way to go.

When I add model4, it looks like the best-fitting previous model is significantly worse-fitting than model4.  This would make sense to me, but I'm worried about an error that this command throws:

> anova(d1_all_fit1, d1_all_fit2, d1_all_fit3, d1_all_fit4)
Chi Square Difference Test

             Df   AIC   BIC   Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
d1_all_fit4 101 23230 23370  619.03
d1_all_fit2 734 56251 56595 5966.77     5347.7     633     <2e-16 ***
d1_all_fit3 737 55341 55673 5062.83     -903.9       3          1
d1_all_fit1 740 56681 57002 6409.26     1346.4       3     <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
Warning message:
In lavTestLRT(object = <S4 object of class "lavaan">, SB.classic = TRUE,  :
  lavaan WARNING: some models are based on a different set of observed variables

I assume that this warning comes from the fact that model4 makes use of only 16 of the 40 observed variables, when the other models make use of all 40.

How big of a problem is this?  Are these models impossible to compare?  E.g., is there something about a simpler model (using fewer observed variables) that will mathematically make it a better fit?  (My intuition is that the reverse would be true, if anything!)

Thanks so much for your help!  Happy to post more of my actual input/output if that would be helpful.

Best wishes,
Kara

messages.subject: Re: "lavaan WARNING: some models are based on a different set of observed variables"
messages.subject_clean: "lavaan WARNING: some models are based on a different set of observed variables"
messages.body_plain:
Kara--
     There multiple problems within these results.  First, yes, using different observed variables in different models makes the chi-square difference test results uninterpretable.  This test requires that the models be nested, one a special case of the next.  Models with different observed variables are not nested.  Even in terms of information criterion indices like AIC, it could be hard to derive value from a comparison of one model with 40 observed variables vs another with 16 observed variables.  The power to reject the 40 variable model will generally be much,much higher.
    There is another problem.  Your anova output shows that your Model2 with 2 factors has fewer DF than your Model3 with 3 factors.  Model2 should be more constrained and have higher DF.  I would very much expect DF(Model1) > DF(Model2) > DF(Model3).  If there are other special features of Model2 not included with Model3, then those two models also are not nested.  Notice that the Model3 chi-square difference is *negative*  This can happen with chi-square differences for nested models from more exotic estimators, but not with ML chi-squares.  I think you may have a syntax error with Model2 and / or Model3.
     There is a bit of literature which argues that models with different numbers of factors may not be suited to chi-square difference tests,because they tend to involve parameter estimates constrained at their boundary.  Discontinuities make the usual chi-square difference p-value untrustworthy.
--Ed Rigdon

http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00273170701329112#.VpwKR_krLrc
--Ed Rigdon

Y be the dependent variable
X be the independent variable
M1 mediator
M2 mediator
I want to test one model where X impacts M1 which impacts Y (a classic mediation), but I also want to test a model where X impacts M1 which impacts M2 which impacts Y. Is this possible, how would one go about doing this?

Any help would be greatly appreciated.
Thank you!

I am trying to do latent change score analysis in Lavaan.

I have two data points--T1 and T2. I cannot fix the error I got--still new to Lavaan. The error message was:

Error in tmp[cbind(REP$row[idx], REP$col[idx])] <- lavpartable$free[idx] :
  NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments

Here is my Lavaan syntax:

model<-"   # Latent variables
           F1 =~ 1*t1var1 + b*t1var2 +s*t1var3
           F2 =~ 1*t2var1 + b*t2var2 +s*t2var3
          # intercept
           t1var1   ~ it1*1
           t2var1   ~ it1*1
           t1var2   ~ ib1*1
           t2var2   ~ ib1*1
           t1var3   ~ is1*1
           t2var3   ~ is1*1
           # covariance
           F1~F2
           # residual variance
           t1var1 ~ t2var1
           t1var2 ~ t2var2
           t1var3 ~ t2var3
           #latent means
           F1 ~0*1  # baseline
           F2 ~1    # difference compared with baseline
           "
 fit  <- cfa(model, data=data, ordered=c("t1var1", "t2var1","t1var2", "t2var2","t1var3", "t2var3"),
            std.lv <http://std.lv/>=FALSE, meanstructure=TRUE, estimator = "WLSMV")

I checked. The variables' names are in standard format. No brackets or other nonstandard symbols.

Anyone has an idea??

Would appreciate any help.

Grace

I think this actually solves most of my problems, including the unexpected differences in the DFs in Model2 vs Model3.  (Thanks for noticing that!)  These are just 4 totally different models with no real relations to each other, and I now see that comparing chi-squares doesn't work for that situation.
> >

> >
> > - Kara

> > On Sunday, January 17, 2016 at 1:20:16 PM UTC-8, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> > > Kara--
> > >      There multiple problems within these results.  First, yes, using different observed variables in different models makes the chi-square difference test results uninterpretable.  This test requires that the models be nested, one a special case of the next.  Models with different observed variables are not nested.  Even in terms of information criterion indices like AIC, it could be hard to derive value from a comparison of one model with 40 observed variables vs another with 16 observed variables.  The power to reject the 40 variable model will generally be much,much higher.
> > >     There is another problem.  Your anova output shows that your Model2 with 2 factors has fewer DF than your Model3 with 3 factors.  Model2 should be more constrained and have higher DF.  I would very much expect DF(Model1) > DF(Model2) > DF(Model3).  If there are other special features of Model2 not included with Model3, then those two models also are not nested.  Notice that the Model3 chi-square difference is *negative*  This can happen with chi-square differences for nested models from more exotic estimators, but not with ML chi-squares.  I think you may have a syntax error with Model2 and / or Model3.
> > >      There is a bit of literature which argues that models with different numbers of factors may not be suited to chi-square difference tests,because they tend to involve parameter estimates constrained at their boundary.  Discontinuities make the usual chi-square difference p-value untrustworthy.
> > > --Ed Rigdon
> > >

> > > >
> > > > When I compare only model1, model2, and model3 (using anova(model1, model2, model3, model4)), I find that model1 fits significantly worse than model3, which is not significantly worse than model2.  So, so far, looks like model3 is the way to go.
> > > >
> > > > When I add model4, it looks like the best-fitting previous model is significantly worse-fitting than model4.  This would make sense to me, but I'm worried about an error that this command throws:
> > > >
> > > > > anova(d1_all_fit1, d1_all_fit2, d1_all_fit3, d1_all_fit4)
> > > > Chi Square Difference Test

> > > > In lavTestLRT(object = <S4 object of class "lavaan">, SB.classic = TRUE,  :
> > > >   lavaan WARNING: some models are based on a different set of observed variables
> > > >
> > > > I assume that this warning comes from the fact that model4 makes use of only 16 of the 40 observed variables, when the other models make use of all 40.
> > > >
> > > > How big of a problem is this?  Are these models impossible to compare?  E.g., is there something about a simpler model (using fewer observed variables) that will mathematically make it a better fit?  (My intuition is that the reverse would be true, if anything!)

> There is one typo for residuals. It should be "~~", not "~".

Same typo here:

           # covariance
           F1~F2

Although for a latent change score, I think you need to regress time 2 on time 1

           F2 ~ F1

and fix the residual for F2 to zero, then define a phantom construct for the F2 residual that represents the change score.

Also, you are imposing invariance constraints on the intercepts, but you are still estimating all intercepts and (implicitly, using the default) fixing the latent means to zero for identification.  So there can't be any latent change in the model as you have specified it -- both means are fixed to zero.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Path model - mediation / lavaan beginner
messages.subject_clean: Path model - mediation / lavaan beginner
messages.body_plain:
SEMNET <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html> would be a good resource for general SEM questions like this.  Short story:  you can't compare models unless they are fit to the same data.  So you need to compare models that include all 4 variables.  Your second model

X -> M1 -> M2 -> Y

includes all 4, but your first model

X -> M1 -> Y

does not.  To rectify this, you just need to find a way to include M2 in the first model, as well, but in a way that doesn't interfere with the simpler hypothesized process.  Including M2 as another endogenous variable, correlated with Y, would be a solution.

X -> M1 -> {M2 <--> Y}
X -> M1 -> M2 -> Y

Or you could just add a regression path from M1 to Y in the second model.  Either way, comparing these 2 nested models would yield a 1-df chi-squared difference test of the null hypothesis that the model with more parameters (top one) fits no better than the "simpler" model with fewer parameters (bottom one).  Rejecting that null would lead you to favor the top model.

Terry

Hi Terry,
Thanks for the response. I was wondering mostly if the model I believe I was fitting, was in fact the model I fit. I believe the model to be appropriate and just want to verify that's what I am fitting. In other words, is the model that I am linking to in that image on Dropbox the same as the lavaan model syntax I have written? I am also happy to take my question to SEMNET.
Thanks for the help,
Chris

>
> Terry

messages.subject: CFA with ordinal data
messages.subject_clean: CFA with ordinal data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

This is my first time using R and the Lavaan package, so I apologize in advance for asking basic questions. Currently, I am trying to fit three nested models on my dataset (23 ordinal variables, 634 observations), and I have run into a few issues I hope you can help me with:

1. I receive >50 'empty cell(s) in bivariate table' warnings, and I am only able to view the first 50. I already read that empty cell warnings are not necessarily bad, but in order to judge this I need to know how many there are. Is there any way I can view all the warnings? Or alternatively, the bivariate frequency tables?
?
2. I would like to incorporate age as a regressor in my models, is this at all possible when doing CFA on ordinal data? Currently, I have tried to have my latent variable(s) covary with age like this:

'factor1 =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + ... + item23
factor1~~age'

However, I get the following error:
Error in tmp[cbind(REP$row[idx], REP$col[idx])] <- lavpartable$free[idx] :
  NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments

What would be the proper way to model this?

3. When analyzing ordinal data, Lavaan does not provide an AIC or BIC. What statistic would you recommend to choose the superior model (as mentioned, the three models are nested )?

Again, I apologize if these are stupid questions, but any help would be greatly appreciated!

Best,

Niels

> is the model that I am linking to in that image on Dropbox the same as the lavaan model syntax I have written?

No, your model (and description) say you want the growth factors to predict P, but your syntax is simply allowing those 3 variables to correlate.  Instead of a double-tilde, use a single tilde.  Also, if you want to interpret the intercept as the mean of C at Time 1, then the first loading on Slope should be 0.

model <-
'
           i =~ 1*C1 + 1*C2 + 1*C3

           s =~ 0*C1 + 1*C2 + 2*C3
           P ~ i + s
 '

Terry

messages.subject: Re: CFA with ordinal data
messages.subject_clean: CFA with ordinal data
messages.body_plain:
> 1. I receive >50 'empty cell(s) in bivariate table' warnings, and I am only able to view the first 50. I already read that empty cell warnings are not necessarily bad, but in order to judge this I need to know how many there are. Is there any way I can view all the warnings? Or alternatively, the bivariate frequency tables?

Use the lavTables() function.  You can provide it your data.frame or your fitted model object (returned by lavaan() or cfa() function), and it will return a data.frame summarizing all the 2-way tables among ordered variables.  Any zero frequencies will be found in rows with 0 under the column "obs.freq"

> 2. I would like to incorporate age as a regressor in my models, is this at all possible when doing CFA on ordinal data?

Yes, regardless of the type of indicator, that is called a MIMIC model (easy to find information by searching Google or SEMNET).

> Currently, I have tried to have my latent variable(s) covary with age like this:
>
> 'factor1 =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + ... + item23
> factor1~~age'

A single tilde is used for regression:    factor1 ~ age

> However, I get the following error:
> Error in tmp[cbind(REP$row[idx], REP$col[idx])] <- lavpartable$free[idx] :
>   NAs are not allowed in subscripted assignments

Not sure what caused this without seeing the full R script, and maybe the data.  Do you get an error when actually regression the factor on age?

> 3. When analyzing ordinal data, Lavaan does not provide an AIC or BIC.

No, those are calculated from log-likelihoods, so by definition they are only available using MLE, not least-squares estimators.

> What statistic would you recommend to choose the superior model (as mentioned, the three models are nested )?

Because the models are nested, you can use the chi-squared difference test, which can be calculated using the anova() function.

> > fit1 <- lavaan(...)
> > fit2 <- lavaan(...)
> > fit3 <- lavaan(...)
> > anova(fit1, fit2, fit3)

For non-nested models, you could compare them using incremental fit indices (e.g., CFI, TLI), as long as they are calculated using a baseline/null model that is nested within all competing models, so that the CFI/TLI places the competing models on the same continuum between a null model and a saturated model.

Terry

A data.frame actually is a special case of a list object, where each list element is (a) an atomic vector and (b) has the same length.  So if leaddata is a list of vectors of the same length,
> > sapply(leaddata, is.atomic)
> > sapply(leaddata, length)
> > all(sapply(leaddata, is.atomic)) # should be TRUE
> > all(sapply(leaddata, length) == sapply(leaddata, length)[1]) # should be TRUE
then you can make it a data.frame like this:

> leadDF <- as.data.frame(leaddata)

A1 =~ c(a,a)*bmi1 + start(.5)*bmi1

bmi2 ~ c(int,int)*1

messages.subject: Re: CFA with ordinal data
messages.subject_clean: CFA with ordinal data
messages.body_plain:
> Could you (or someone else) confirm that I am correctly controlling for age when entering the following syntax?:
>
> 'factor1 =~ item1 + ... + item12
> factor2 =~ item13 + ... + item23
> factor1~age
> factor2~age'

Well, you are using age to predict each factor, that is correct.  But the term "control" indicates that you want to estimate the effects of a predictor (say X) on an outcome (say Y) when holding a covariate (here, age) constant.  What effects are you interested in estimating while controlling for age?  So far, you are estimating the effect of age on each factor, and the effects of the factors on their indicators, so you are saying that age only affects the indicators indirectly via the factors (you can think of the factors as mediators in this circumstance). But there is no "controlling" going on, so that may not be what you mean.

In the CFA without age, the only predictors are latent factors, and the only outcomes are observed indicators.  To estimate the effect of factors on indicators (i.e., factor loadings) while controlling for age, then you should regress the indicators on age.  Because you haven't observed the latent factor, the model will not be identified if you try to simultaneously estimate the effect of age on the factors and on all indicators, so you need to choose at least one indicator per factor that is not regressed on age (or you can fit a series of models, regressing one item at a time on age).  When you regress the factors on age, this is called the MIMIC method for detecting differential item functioning (DIF; also called measurement bias or noninvariance); or you can use restricted factor analysis (RFA), in which you allow the factors to correlate with age instead of estimating those relationships regression slopes -- they are equivalent models, so they lead to the same conclusions, but you can probably find more literature on the MIMIC method.  Here are some links to get started:

MIMIC:  http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s10862-008-9118-9
RFA:  http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705519809540095

Terry

> For a follow-up question, if I want to convert these mean differences to a Cohen's d-type effect size, would I just divide the mean difference by the square root of the variance of the latent for my non-reference group?

It depends.  Actual Cohen's d is divided by the square-root of the pooled variance (use the same as for the t test formula for unequal Ns/variances).  Glass' delta was developed with treatment-control designs in mind, and it divides by the control-group's SD, because treatments can change the spread as well as the location of data.  I would be inclined to use the reference group's SD, since that group (with latent M = 0) is the reference group to which you are comparing the latent M = -0.71

If you test whether latent variances can be constrained to equality and cannot reject the null, then you only have one SD to work with, which would make the choice simpler.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Equality constraints on standardized estimates
messages.subject_clean: Equality constraints on standardized estimates
messages.body_plain:
> I was wondering whether it would be possible to equality constrain standardized coefficients?

You could define standardized estimates as new parameters in your model syntax, then try constraining those to equality.  You standardize a regression slope by multiplying the raw slope by the ratio of SD(predictor) / SD(outcome), regardless of the number of predictors.  If they are observed variables, it is easy to check your descriptive stats and directly enter a numerical value.  Here is a toy example:

> (S <- matrix(c(2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 0, 0, 0, 5), 3, 3,
>              dimnames = list(c("x1","x2","e"), c("x1","x2","e"))))
> set.seed(123)
> (dat <- as.data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(n = 50, mu = c(0, 0, 0), Sigma = S)))
> dat$y <- 10 + 3*dat$x1 + 4*dat$x2 + dat$e
> head(dat)
> sapply(dat, var) # use these values in the model syntax below
> model0 <- ' ## regression model
>   y ~ b1*x1 + b2*x2
>   ## define standardized estimates
>   ## denominator = total observed variance of y
>   ## numerators = observed variances of x1 & x2
>   b1s := b1 * sqrt(1.519002 / 75.506641)
>   b2s := b2 * sqrt(2.799830 / 75.506641)
> '
> ## notice the newly defined parameters match the standardized output
> fit0 <- sem(model0, data = dat)
> summary(fit0, standardized = TRUE)
> ## now test this constraint
> model1 <- c(model0, ' b1s == b2s ')
> fit1 <- sem(model1, data = dat)
> summary(fit1, standardized = TRUE) # raw slopes differ, std. slopes are ==
> anova(fit0, fit1) # reject the null

If either is a latent variable, then the estimated variance of the latent predictor is a model parameter that is easily labeled and used in the equation for the defined (standardized) parameters.  If the outcome is latent, then you will need to define the total variance of the outcome as a sum of the estimated (and labeled) residual variance plus the model-implied explained variance (tracing rules or matrix algebra will help you here) -- then you use that defined parameter in the equation for the defined (standardized) parameters.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: logLik in sem output is NA
messages.subject_clean: logLik in sem output is NA
messages.body_plain:
> 1) I thought that the chi-square test statistic was basically a function of log likelihood at the maximum, so I don't understand why I got chisq but not logLik.

That is unexpected, since you are using MLE.  Without a logLik, AIC and BIC can't be calculated, but if chi-squared is provided, then any fit index based on chi-squared can also be calculated.  Can you provide enough data (and script) to reproduce the problem?

> 2) In general, I don't understand why fmin (from fit.measures) is different from logLik, since I assumed that logLik was the log likelihood at the maximum.

fmin * N = the chi-squared value (i.e., the likelihood-ratio test), which -2 times the difference between 2 different log-likelihoods: the likelihood of the data under the target model (H0), and the likelihood of the data under the saturated model (H1).  fmin is not itself a log-likelihood or a likelihood ratio, just a shortcut software developers used to calculate the LRT statistic from complete-data summary statistics rather than calculating and summing the N log-likelihoods for both H0 and H1 models, then calculating the difference of the sums.  I don't know why you aren't getting a logLik for converged models, but fmin is a function of the observed and model-implied summary statistics, so it can be calculated using model parameters -- no need for likelihoods (unless you have missing data).

> 3) When the regression piece of a sem model consists solely of manifest variables, how does the model get estimated? Is it different from sem models with latent independent variables?

The default is fixed.x = FALSE, so the (co)variances of exogenous predictors are not estimated.  In your example, the multinormal likelihood (given the model parameters) of the 9 endogenous variables would be calculated conditional on fixed values of the 3 exogenous variables (like residual likelihood?).   You can choose to treat the predictors as random variables by setting fixed.x = TRUE, in which case the multinormal likelihood (given the model parameters) of all 12 variables is calculated.  Is logLik missing for either or both of these settings?  Again, a reproducible example is the only way to get to the bottom of it.  And check that you are using the latest version of lavaan (0.5-20:

> sessionInfo()

Terry

> I can see very easily how to test the above models compared to the confirg model, using anova, but to what does one compare the config model to see if adding the configural constraints had a significant effect?  I tried anova(cfa.no.group , cfa.config)

That is not "adding configural constraints" -- the no-groups model is essentially your most restricted multiple-group model, in the sense that you assume all parameters are equivalent across groups.  So cfa.no.group is actually nested within cfa.config, not the other way around.  (But to get that chi-squared difference using anova(), you would have to fit cfa.no.group as a multigroup model where all parameters are constrained to equality.)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Yves,

The usual modeling framework that comes to mind in distinguishing population averaged from individual level is generalized estimating equations: basically a marginal modeling approach using robust (sandwich based) Huber White variance estimators. The original article from Liang and Zeger 1973 describes estimating equations, sandwich errors, and their asymptotic properties. One of their advantages is that they provide consistent error estimation regardless of correct model specification, or any kind of parametric model for the errors.

I'm a little hesitant to suggest sandwich errors would be appropriate in an SEM framework. One of the key assumptions to SEM, in my mind, is the nature of the underlying normal distribution of endogenous or exogenous variables so that 0 covariance implies conditional independence.

messages.subject_clean: Mean structure question
messages.body_plain:
> When I obtain the means from the summary(fit.invariance[[3]]), all the means have different estimates. How would I get the estimates for the means that are constrained across groups?

You can find them in the constrained model, which was used to test whether those constraints are tenable:  fit.invariance[[4]] (or fit.invariance[[5]] if you set strict = FALSE)

> As mentioned previously, the summary(cfa.fit) will only give 0.000 for the mean estimates of the latents, even when using group.equal=c("means","intercepts").

The default method for identifying the mean structure with latent variables is to set the latent means/intercepts to zero (regardless of whether std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE or FALSE).  When you constrain indicator intercepts to equality across groups, that allows you to estimate all but 1 of the groups' latent means.  To test whether the latent means are the same, you constrain them to equality -- because you need to identify the latent means, constraining them to equality means constraining them to all == 0.  You can estimate equality-constrained latent means if you identify them by choosing a reference indicator and set its intercept (across groups) to zero.  But ultimately, that just makes your latent means equal to (equality-constrained) indicator means.  You could also use the effects-coding method of identification (constrain the indicator intercepts to average 0, so you can estimate all intercepts and latent means), but the location of an unobserved distribution on the real-number line is arbitrary, so I don't think it buys you any interpretability to constrain estimated latent means instead of constraining them all to a fixed quantity.

Terry

Yes, the same syntax rules still apply.  You just specify the regression paths that you want to freely estimate, and label them the same way to define indirect effects of interest.  Optionally, you can also estimate the residual covariances among

> M1 ~~ M2 + M3
> M2 ~~ M3

I would recommend estimating these parameters by default, unless your theory really posits that the only reason those variables covary is because they share X as a common cause.  You can always test whether they are zero by comparing models where they are constrained vs. free.

I would certainly expect a model with 37 ordinal indicators to run slowly, but I think this is compounded by the fact that your indicators all have 7 categories.  This is why it is so helpful to provide the data and script that cause a problem.  Your models run fine when you treat the data as continuous, although you should still use a robust estimator (MLR) to adjust for non-normality.  With 5 or more categories, you can expect comparable results whether you treat data as ordered or continuous (read this article <http://psych.colorado.edu/~willcutt/pdfs/Rhemtulla_2012.pdf> for details), but the latter method tends to cause fewer problems like the ones you encountered.  Now, the only warnings are that there are 2 missing values of gender (you can safely ignore that), and that the latent covariance matrix is not positive definite.  The cause of this appears to be redundancy among at least 2 factors (correlations approaching 1, sometimes exceeding 1 -- see my comments at the bottom of the attachment).

I cleaned up your code to make it more legible, in case you ever need to post more syntax in the future.  There are also many tricks to making it shorter and easier to read, which I hope are helpful to you as well (e.g., using paste() instead of typing out 37 variable names, read.csv() already imports a data.frame so you don't have to make another data.frame out of it).

Reading through the lavaan tutorial pages also might help you learn how to read Sunthud's example syntax files:

messages.subject_clean: CFA with ordinal data
messages.body_plain:
Op vrijdag 22 januari 2016 13:20:20 UTC+1 schreef Terrence Jorgensen:

> > Could you (or someone else) confirm that I am correctly controlling for age when entering the following syntax?:
> >
> > 'factor1 =~ item1 + ... + item12
> > factor2 =~ item13 + ... + item23
> > factor1~age
> > factor2~age'
>
> Well, you are using age to predict each factor, that is correct.  But the term "control" indicates that you want to estimate the effects of a predictor (say X) on an outcome (say Y) when holding a covariate (here, age) constant.  What effects are you interested in estimating while controlling for age?  So far, you are estimating the effect of age on each factor, and the effects of the factors on their indicators, so you are saying that age only affects the indicators indirectly via the factors (you can think of the factors as mediators in this circumstance). But there is no "controlling" going on, so that may not be what you mean.
>
> In the CFA without age, the only predictors are latent factors, and the only outcomes are observed indicators.  To estimate the effect of factors on indicators (i.e., factor loadings) while controlling for age, then you should regress the indicators on age.  Because you haven't observed the latent factor, the model will not be identified if you try to simultaneously estimate the effect of age on the factors and on all indicators, so you need to choose at least one indicator per factor that is not regressed on age (or you can fit a series of models, regressing one item at a time on age).  When you regress the factors on age, this is called the MIMIC method for detecting differential item functioning (DIF; also called measurement bias or noninvariance); or you can use restricted factor analysis (RFA), in which you allow the factors to correlate with age instead of estimating those relationships regression slopes -- they are equivalent models, so they lead to the same conclusions, but you can probably find more literature on the MIMIC method.  Here are some links to get started:
>
> MIMIC:  http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s10862-008-9118-9
> RFA:  http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705519809540095
>
> Terry

Dear Terry,

Thank you very much for the advice and the recommendations, I am going to look into it!

Best,

Niels

messages.body_plain:
I have been called on this. Yes, it is right that the mr/mplus can return a negative chi-square. This is not too common, but mostly happens with simple models with very good fit, its simlar to when you find a TLI higher than 1, its not common but it can happend
The mr formula doesnt has anything that prevents it from being negative, while the lmrr does prevents the chi-square to be negative.
If interested, we compare this conditions of negative chi-square to Mplus, and Mplus doesnt report the chi-square when this happens, and doesnt tells you that it was negative, it looks like some error happend but you dont know why. With MR\Mplus it can happend that the combine chi-squre can not be estimated, with runMI you can distinguish these conditions from a negative value, not in mplus.
LMRR is there as an alternative specially in conditions when MR cannot be computed

Still,in general common circunstances the MR is a better method to combine the ch-square (we still have to finish the paper talking about this).
The other fit indices are estimates from the combine chi-square of the model and the combine chi-square of the null model. There are no good guidelines on how to combines the other fit indices, or if calculating them from the combine chi-squares are the best option. We follow this convention in runMI since it seems like the less risky method so far. We need more research about it.

Wow thank you so much Terrence!  You have been so kind to me!  I have tried what you suggested and it all works, and it all makes sense!  It looks like in the whole sample (male and female combined) there was a very strong correlation between Loss of Control and Tolerance of 0.859, which is not strong enough to produce non positive definite matrix of latent variables.  This correlation became all the more noticeable when I used measurementInvarianceCat to compare males to females, because among females, the correlation between these variable was even higher, and the size of the correlated became out of bounds at 1.002 for females as calculated from (cor.means <- inspect(MI.gender[["fit.means"]], "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>")), which explains why the correlation matrix of latent variables was not positive definite for females when they were being compared to males.  I now definitely have my answer: there is not even configural measurement invariance for gender with the scale among New Zealand smokers.  A study failed to replicate the factor structure among Spanish speaking Latino smokers in Texas due to  high intercorrelations (>.90)  among the Loss of Control, Craving, Tolerance, and Cue Exposure subscales, and another USA study also found high correlations between factors.
Thank you so much for you help and especially for taking the time to teach me about statistics in general and writing more beautiful R code in particular.  This is vital to the veracity of the results because, as Keats noted,
'Beauty is truth, truth beauty,—that is all

On 01/27/2016 09:13 AM, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
>     I would like to  calculate calculate the chi-squared difference test
>     by hand (using the formula described here:
>     https://www.statmodel.com/chidiff.shtml

This procedure is only valid when test = "Satorra.Bentler" (or estimator
= "MLM", or "WLSM")

This particular version of the scaled difference test is implemented in
lavaan using lavTestLRT(fit1, fit2, test = "satorra.bentler.2001").

You could indeed compute this by hand, and you should get the same
result as the output of lavTestLRT, in this case.

But WLSMV uses the Satterthwaite adjustment (mean AND variance
adjusted). This calls for a different scaled test statistic, which
corresponds to lavTestLRT(fit1, fit2, test = "satorra.2000").

Computing this by hand would be, well, a challenge. But of course, you
can look at the source code to see how things are done.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Multiple mediation with parallel and serial paths
messages.body_plain:
> Thank you. In that case, would the following model be appropriate? If so, which values would I multiply to obtain the indirect effects?

Yes, but you have specified some of the same paths twice.  The paths labeled {j, k, l} are the same as those labeled {m, n, o}.  Read the tutorial to see how to calculate indirect effects:   http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

> In regards to estimating the residual covariances, I need to incorporate that into my original model as well. Would I estimate those parameters for each mediator?

Yes, yes.

> When I have five mediators in parallel would it be each mediator covaried with each of the other mediators?

I'm not sure what you mean by parallel or serial.  In your first model, Set 1 predicts Set 2, which then predicts Set 3:

{X} --> {M1, M2, M3, M4} --> {Y}

In your second model, Set 1 predicts Set 2, which predicts Set 3, which predicts Set 4:

{X} --> {M1, M2, M3} --> {M4} --> {Y}

Either way, variables within the same {Set} can have residual correlations freely estimated without worrying about empirical under-identification.  If you don't have clear sets like this, then it can get more complicated.  If by "5 in parallel" you mean

X --> M1 --> M2 --> M3 --> M4 --> Y

then you would not specify any residual correlations, because they could result in feedback loops (a non-recursive model).

> In your example you have M1~~M2+M3, why do you have those added?

In lavaan syntax, the "+" operator means "and", just like in your regressions when you have more than one predictor of an outcome:

Y ~ X + M1 + M2 + M3 + M4

Terry

On Tuesday, January 26, 2016 at 5:15:00 AM UTC-5, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > When I obtain the means from the summary(fit.invariance[[3]]), all the means have different estimates. How would I get the estimates for the means that are constrained across groups?
>
> You can find them in the constrained model, which was used to test whether those constraints are tenable:  fit.invariance[[4]] (or fit.invariance[[5]] if you set strict = FALSE)
>
> > As mentioned previously, the summary(cfa.fit) will only give 0.000 for the mean estimates of the latents, even when using group.equal=c("means","intercepts").
>
> The default method for identifying the mean structure with latent variables is to set the latent means/intercepts to zero (regardless of whether std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE or FALSE).  When you constrain indicator intercepts to equality across groups, that allows you to estimate all but 1 of the groups' latent means.  To test whether the latent means are the same, you constrain them to equality -- because you need to identify the latent means, constraining them to equality means constraining them to all == 0.  You can estimate equality-constrained latent means if you identify them by choosing a reference indicator and set its intercept (across groups) to zero.  But ultimately, that just makes your latent means equal to (equality-constrained) indicator means.  You could also use the effects-coding method of identification (constrain the indicator intercepts to average 0, so you can estimate all intercepts and latent means), but the location of an unobserved distribution on the real-number line is arbitrary, so I don't think it buys you any interpretability to constrain estimated latent means instead of constraining them all to a fixed quantity.
>
> Terry

messages.body_plain:
On 01/28/2016 10:56 AM, Marcos Angelini wrote:
> Dear Yves,
>
> I think there is an error when you set fixed.x = T because it does not
> free the parameters that it suppose. Here a proof:

It is not supposed to. When fixed.x = TRUE, we just take the 'x'-part of
the model for what it is: a set of correlated exogenous variables. This
means that we simply copy the 'x' part of the observed covariance
matrix, and plug it in the implied covariance matrix.

Why would we need to fix those covariances to zero?

Only when fixed.x = FALSE, the covariances between the exogenous
covariates become model parameters, and you can (if you believe this is
a good idea) fixed them to zero in the syntax.

Yves.

When you have a multiple-group model, predict() does not return a single matrix that can be coerced into a data.frame, but rather a list of matrices (one for each group).  So you can stack them into a single matrix using rbind(), then convert to a data.frame

> fscores <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, predict(fit.pa3dim22.3)))

predict() doesn't return the group id's, so you can add them afterward if you need them.

> fscores$group <- rep(fit.pa3dim22.3@Dat...@group.label, times = fit.pa3dim22.3@Data@nobs)

Terry

I tried running the model but I am not sure which is the correct approach. Based on reading some of the help responses here, I tried two method. My predictors are categorical (0/1), so  I used the MLR estimator because I do not have enough sample size (n=515) to use WLS estimator.

            '

model.two.6 <- cfa(model.h, data=finIQ.6, estimator = "MLR", std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)
summary(model.two.6, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
